claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles with partial short-range ordering on carbon supports remain structurally and chemically stable during redox cycling at 773–1173 K.
Short-range clustering occurs locally at the carbon–nanoparticle interface.
Interfacial short-range clustering reduces surface diffusion.
Reduced surface diffusion suppresses elemental segregation.
Reduced surface diffusion suppresses nanoparticle coarsening.
The proposed initial material consists of approximately 5–10 nm near-equiatomic CoNiFeCu solid-solution nanoparticles with partial short-range ordering on carbon.
Defective carbon sites can anchor metallic nanoparticles through partial intercalation and rooting at graphite edge planes.
Strong nanoparticle–defective-carbon interactions provide thermal stability.
Anchoring at defective carbon reduces the diffusion of mobile species.
Reduced mobile-species diffusion prevents severe composition fluctuations and structural transformations.
Locally correlated multi-element arrangements at the carbon–metal interface pin the nanoparticle structure during high-temperature redox cycling.
Partial short-range ordering preserves near-equiatomic composition and single-phase character by mitigating element-specific oxidation.
Ordered carbon-supported nanoparticles will undergo less grain growth, segregation, and phase formation than less-ordered or unsupported analogues.
Nanoparticles lacking short-range order or carbon anchoring will show significant segregation, morphology changes, or partial phase separation under equivalent conditions.
Above approximately 1300 K, short-range order or carbon anchoring may no longer prevent de-mixing or coarsening.
Strongly oxidizing atmospheres may overcome the stabilization supplied by short-range order or carbon anchoring.
